parent.name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nc3 Nf6 3. f4 d5 4. fxe5 Nxe4 5. Qf3 f5
parent.overview: White plays f4 on the third move, a King's Gambit structure with the knight already on c3 protecting e4 and d5. Black's usual answers are 3...d5, 3...exf4 and 3...d6; the sources agree 3...d5 is the principled antidote. After 4.fxe5 Nxe4 the position is material-equal (White traded the f-pawn for the e-pawn) and White chooses between 5.Nf3 (Breyer, the most common, roughly balanced and comfortable for Black), 5.Qf3 (Spielmann, with Ben Finegold behind it, but called flawed after 5...Nc6) and 5.d3 (Oxford, with the Würzburger Trap 5...Qh4+ 6.g3 Nxg3 7.Nf3 Qh5 8.Nxd5). If Black accepts with 3...exf4, 4.e5 chases the f6-knight back to g8, giving White a lead in development; Wikipedia says Black should not accept, while a beginner guide says White regains the pawn quickly. The gambit scores well at club level and is considered too risky at grandmaster level.

parent.name: Van't Kruijs Opening
parent.overview: 1.e3 opens lines for the f1-bishop and the queen, claims the e4 square lightly and commits to nothing else; it blocks the c1-bishop, so White plans to free that bishop early (b3, or d4 and Nd2/Bd2). It is mainly a transposition device: c4 gives English-type positions, d4 Queen's Pawn structures, b3 Larsen's Opening, and f4 Bird-type set-ups, and 1...e5 2.e4 is a reversed Open Game. Black has maximum freedom and the opening invites him to over-commit in the centre. It is considered passive but sound and gives White no particular advantage; its popularity has declined and strong players use it mainly to reach known structures.

parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: Mieses Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.d3, releasing the c1-bishop and making only a modest claim on the centre, and usually heads for an Indian-type set-up with g3, Nf3, Bg2 and short castling, then strikes with e4 (or c4). It generally transposes to the King's Indian Attack (after g3 and Nf3), the Closed Sicilian, or to colour-reversed Pirc, Modern or Philidor structures, so Black can occupy the centre with ...d5 and ...e5 and develop comfortably. Chess Doctrine calls it objectively passive: Black equalises quickly, theory load is minimal, and it is mainly a surprise weapon in rapid and blitz. Kasparov chose it against Deep Blue in 1997 (Game 3) to avoid computer preparation, but at grandmaster level it remains the exception. The play is closed and manoeuvring.

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.
